profiles.meeting_scenario: The simulation platform team and the numerical methods team are holding a coordination meeting to align on how Verificarlo CI will be added to the existing GitHub Actions pipeline for a C++/Fortran numerical optimization codebase. The context is that the numerical team wants earlier detection of floating-point regressions, while the platform team needs a workable handoff for runners, artifacts, and ownership of the new CI lane before the next release branch is cut in two weeks. The agenda is to confirm what the first Verificarlo CI integration will run, what artifact the numerical team will consume, how results will be compared against a baseline, and who owns follow-up changes after the initial setup. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the interface between the two workstreams: the platform team will expose a CI job and artifacts, and the numerical team will plug in analysis thresholds and start reviewing regressions.

members.name: Priya Natarajan
members.expertise: CI/CD pipelines, reproducible toolchains, GitHub Actions, containerized builds
members.background: Priya maintains the organization-wide build infrastructure for HPC-adjacent repositories and recently migrated several projects from Jenkins to GitHub Actions with reusable workflows and artifact retention rules.
members.private_state: Priya wants the integration to fit the existing shared CI model with minimal new infrastructure, avoid adding a blocking job that flakes on pull requests, and keep ownership boundaries clear so her team is not responsible for interpreting numerical output.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'baseline', they mean a reproducible artifact generated from the current main branch in CI, not an older externally curated reference run.
A 'CI integration' should start as a non-blocking workflow attached to pull requests and promoted later only if it proves reliable.
Using the 'same environment as the current pipeline' means the standard GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runner plus the repository's container image.
The platform team's deliverable ends at publishing raw Verificarlo output and logs; downstream interpretation belongs to the numerical team.

members.name: Leo Marchand
members.expertise: floating-point analysis, numerical optimization, Monte Carlo arithmetic, scientific code validation
members.background: Leo works on stability and reproducibility of large simulation kernels and has previously used Verificarlo offline on a lab cluster to diagnose cancellation and sensitivity issues in solver components.
members.private_state: Leo wants the new workflow to catch subtle regressions without forcing scientists to run separate validation scripts manually, and he hopes the platform team will operationalize enough of the analysis that developers can trust alerts without deep numerical expertise.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'baseline', they mean the vetted golden reference run the team saved from the latest release candidate built with the production compiler stack.
If something is 'in CI', developers will see an actionable regression summary on every pull request rather than having to inspect raw artifacts later.
Using the 'same environment as the current pipeline' means the same compiler family, math libraries, and CPU characteristics as the team's self-hosted performance-validation node.
The first rollout should already include the small validation pack the scientists use for regression sign-off, because that is the obvious minimum meaningful coverage for numerical drift.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss 'comparing against the baseline' as if it names one obvious reference.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the baseline is a fresh artifact produced from the current main branch by the new CI workflow, so comparisons are branch-to-branch within the same infrastructure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the baseline is the team's curated golden run from the latest release candidate on the production-style toolchain, so comparisons are against a historically trusted numerical reference.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In software coordination meetings, 'baseline' sounds like settled shared vocabulary, and both interpretations are perfectly standard in their respective workstreams, so neither person expects ambiguity.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the first CI lane
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to putting Verificarlo 'into CI' and starting with the 'small validation pack'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 takes this to mean one lightweight subset of the repository's existing smoke tests that can run quickly on pull requests, with broader numerical coverage deferred to a nightly job.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 takes this to mean the scientist-maintained mini validation pack used for numerical sign-off, which is still 'small' by research standards but larger and more expensive than the smoke suite.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sides sincerely think they are converging on an intentionally modest first step, and the phrase 'small validation pack' feels descriptive enough that neither enumerates the exact test list.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the new run should use 'the same environment as the current pipeline' so results are comparable.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the job will execute on the standard GitHub Actions runner inside the repository's container image, because that is the operational definition of the current pipeline for her team.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the job will execute on the self-hosted AVX2 validation node with the usual GCC/OpenBLAS stack, because that is the environment whose numerical behavior the team actually trusts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both environments are genuinely part of the project's broader automation landscape, so the phrase 'current pipeline' plausibly refers to either one depending on whether the speaker is thinking about CI infrastructure or numerical validation practice.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the handoff should produce an 'actionable report' for developers.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks an actionable report means raw Verificarlo outputs, logs, and a preserved artifact that Leo's team can inspect when something changes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks an actionable report means a summarized per-kernel drift view with pass/fail interpretation or at least highlighted suspicious deltas directly visible from the pull request.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations are compatible with the ordinary software phrase 'actionable', and because they are discussing ownership boundaries rather than report layout explicitly, the divergence hides under apparent agreement about helping developers.

turns.inner_thought: I need a clean handoff before the release branch freezes. The safest path is to add one reusable GitHub Actions job that stays non-blocking on pull requests until we know it doesn't flake. I also want to keep ownership crisp: my team can stand up the lane, manage artifacts, and keep it reproducible, but we should not become the group deciding whether a numerical wobble matters.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want to get aligned on the Verificarlo handoff today so we can wire a new job into the repo before the release branch cut. From my side, I'd like to leave with a clear first slice, what we publish out of the run, how we're comparing against the baseline, and where the platform piece ends versus where your team takes over.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that's exactly the interface we need. The value is catching drift on every PR against the vetted golden reference from the latest release-candidate run, not waiting until someone remembers to rerun the lab-cluster validation. If we can anchor on that baseline, reviewers can spot subtle regressions much earlier.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. The main thing I want is earlier visibility into floating-point drift by comparing each change against the baseline instead of finding out later during manual validation. If we can get that feedback loop into the normal review path, it'll save us a lot of last-minute digging.

turns.inner_thought: Let's start small and operationally safe: one lightweight subset of the existing smoke coverage on PRs, measure runtime and artifact volume, then we can talk about nightlies or broader packs later. Saying 'small validation pack' should land well; everyone usually means the initial trimmed set.
turns.utterance: Agreed. My suggestion would be to start conservatively by putting Verificarlo into CI on the small validation pack first, just so we can get a read on runtime, artifact size, and how noisy the outputs are before we widen anything.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, the scientist-maintained mini pack is the obvious minimum. It's not huge, but it does cover the solver and advection cases where Monte Carlo arithmetic actually tells us something useful. If that pack is in CI from day one, we get meaningful detection instead of a demo lane.
turns.utterance: I think that's the right first slice too. The small validation pack already exercises the sensitive solver and advection kernels the scientists keep an eye on, so it should be enough to make the signal worth trusting without trying to do everything at once.

turns.inner_thought: I can reuse the existing Actions workflow and container setup on the standard hosted runner; that's the current pipeline in practical terms for me. Reusing that path keeps maintenance low and makes the run reproducible in the same CI infrastructure, which is exactly what we want for comparisons.
turns.utterance: On implementation, I can keep the results comparable by running the new lane in the same environment as the current pipeline and hanging it off the existing reusable workflow. That way we're not inventing a separate path just for this.

turns.inner_thought: Great, if it stays on the validation node setup with the usual compiler family and math libraries, the baseline will still mean what we think it means. CPU behavior and library details matter here, so keeping the same environment is exactly what I was hoping to hear.
turns.utterance: Yes, using the same environment should make the baseline meaningful. The more we preserve the compiler and math-library behavior people already rely on, the easier it'll be to separate real drift from setup differences.

turns.inner_thought: I should frame the deliverable in developer-friendly CI terms without committing us to numerical interpretation. A PR-triggered job, outputs uploaded as artifacts, links on the checks page—that is an actionable report from a platform standpoint and keeps the responsibility boundary intact.
turns.utterance: What I can commit to from the platform side is a pull-request-triggered job that uploads the Verificarlo outputs and links them from the checks page, so developers have an actionable report right where they're already looking.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—if the PR check surfaces a kernel-level drift summary with the suspicious deltas called out, reviewers won't need to dig through raw logs. That's the whole point of getting this into CI rather than leaving it as a specialist-only artifact.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. If the actionable report highlights the drift by kernel, reviewers should be able to tell pretty quickly whether a change looks numerically suspicious or just within the expected spread.

turns.inner_thought: We seem aligned: my team sets up the workflow, emits raw outputs, and stores the first main-branch artifact as the baseline; Leo's team can layer on thresholds and interpretation after that. I need to keep saying this in a way that confirms the handoff without reopening ownership questions.
turns.utterance: Okay, then let me summarize what I'm hearing: my team will wire the workflow and publish the artifacts, and your team can plug in the threshold logic once the first baseline run is in place. That should give us a clean interface and let us move without blocking on all the interpretation details up front.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine. I'll send the kernels we expect from the scientist validation pack and the reference numbers from the golden run so they can line things up this week. Once their CI lane is there, we can attach thresholds and get useful PR-level regressions quickly.
turns.utterance: Works for me. I'll send over the expected kernels and reference numbers from the validation pack so we can move ahead this week, and then we should have what we need to start comparing against the baseline as soon as the lane is up.
